<!-- unit doc:docs/jobs.md#enqueuing-jobs -->
**Source:** `docs/jobs.md` § Enqueuing Jobs (in "Jobs")

#### Enqueuing Jobs

```typescript
import { enqueueJob } from '#/jobs/enqueue';

await enqueueJob('sendWebhook', {
  subscriptionId: sub.id,
  action: 'create',
  resourceId: record.id,
  data: record,
});

// With options
await enqueueJob('myJob', payload, {
  delay: 5000,        // Delay in ms
  priority: 1,        // Lower = higher priority
  attempts: 3,        // Retry attempts
  type: 'adhoc',      // 'cron' | 'cronTrigger' | 'adhoc' (default adhoc)
  lane: 'slow',       // 'fast' | 'slow' — overrides the handler's declared lane (see Fast and Slow Lanes)
  bypass: false,      // skip the overflow buffer — latency-critical jobs go straight to BullMQ
});
```

A custom `jobId` must satisfy BullMQ's rules (`validateJobId`): not `'0'`, no `'0:'` prefix, no `':'`. An invalid id throws at enqueue rather than being quarantined later.

When overflow is active, an `adhoc` enqueue returns `{ jobId, name, outboxed: true }` (spilled to the buffer) instead of adding to BullMQ directly. See [Overflow Buffer](#overflow-buffer).

A keyed singleton (or a singleton's cron run) is added with BullMQ's `deduplication` id (see [Singleton Job](#singleton-job)): while one exists, another add is a no-op.

In test (`isTest`), `enqueueJob` skips BullMQ entirely and runs the handler inline — cascading effects happen for real, errors propagate, no queue/overflow machinery involved. The inline job still receives the resolved envelope (lane included). To test routing, call `enqueueOrSpill` directly (see `jobs/tests/`).

<!-- unit doc:docs/jobs.md#fast-and-slow-lanes -->
**Source:** `docs/jobs.md` § Fast and Slow Lanes (in "Jobs")

#### Fast and Slow Lanes

One large send is thousands of jobs on the same worker pool every other kind of work shares; in plain FIFO order, everything else waits behind it. Slow work instead waits in the same queue at the lowest priority, so fast work is always picked first; it runs in at most its share of each worker's slots, so the rest stay free for fast work; and it may fill only its share of the queue's depth budget.

<!-- unit doc:docs/jobs.md#fast-and-slow-lanes/choosing-a-lane -->
**Source:** `docs/jobs.md` § Fast and Slow Lanes › Choosing a Lane (in "Jobs")

##### Choosing a Lane

A lane is a label on the job envelope (`JobData.lane`, next to `type`), not a kind of job. `buildJobData` resolves it once, where every producer builds the envelope: the request's lane, then the enqueue option, then the handler's declared default, then `fast`.

```typescript
export const bulkThing = makeJob<Payload>(async (ctx, payload) => { ... }, { lane: JobLane.slow });
```

A producer that knows the work's size sets the lane per enqueue instead — `sendEmail` puts its per-recipient `deliverEmail` fan-out on the slow lane when it has more than `EMAIL_SLOW_LANE_MIN_RECIPIENTS` recipients (`fanOutLane`), and keeps smaller sends fast. Every `queue.add` site stamps the lane (and the slow lane's priority): `enqueueJob`, `upsertCronJobScheduler` (used by `registerCronJobs` and the `cronJobSync` hook), and the drain. The superadmin enqueue (`options.lane`) and cron trigger (`{ lane }` body) accept an override. The worker reads only `job.data.lane`; an envelope with no lane (queued before lanes existed) is fast everywhere.

`makeSingletonJob` and `makeSupersedingJob` carry the wrapped handler's declared lane.

<!-- unit doc:docs/jobs.md#fast-and-slow-lanes/priority-fast-work-is-always-picked-first -->
**Source:** `docs/jobs.md` § Fast and Slow Lanes › Priority: Fast Work Is Always Picked First (in "Jobs")

##### Priority: Fast Work Is Always Picked First

BullMQ moves a job to active from the plain wait list first and from the prioritized set only when the wait list is empty. Slow jobs are added with `priority: SLOW_LANE_PRIORITY` (`2^21 - 1`, one below BullMQ's `PRIORITY_LIMIT`) by `withLanePriority` (`jobs/lanePriority.ts`), which every add site applies. BullMQ scores a prioritized job `priority × 2^32 + counter` in a Redis double; at `PRIORITY_LIMIT` that passes `2^53`, equal-priority jobs collide, and the slow lane loses its FIFO order. The admin enqueue caps `priority` at `SLOW_LANE_PRIORITY` for the same reason. So a fast job never queues behind a slow backlog, and a job given an explicit priority (the admin enqueue accepts one) is served after all unprioritized fast work and, below `SLOW_LANE_PRIORITY`, ahead of all slow work; at `SLOW_LANE_PRIORITY` it waits and counts as slow work. Within one priority BullMQ keeps FIFO order.

<!-- unit doc:docs/jobs.md#fast-and-slow-lanes/slots-slow-work-uses-at-most-its-share -->
**Source:** `docs/jobs.md` § Fast and Slow Lanes › Slots: Slow Work Uses at Most Its Share (in "Jobs")

##### Slots: Slow Work Uses at Most Its Share

Priority decides which job starts next, but BullMQ never preempts a running job, so ordering alone would let slow work fill every slot and make a fast job wait for a slow one to finish. Each worker therefore runs slow jobs in at most `JOBS_SLOW_SLOT_FRACTION` of its `JOBS_WORKER_CONCURRENCY` slots (at least one), counted by the worker's own `SlowSlotPool` (`jobs/slowSlotPool.ts`). When a slow job starts on a worker whose slow share is full, `claimSlotOrRequeue` (`jobs/claimSlotOrRequeue.ts`) parks it: it moves to delayed and returns to the slow band at its stored priority when it comes due. `moveToDelayed` skips the attempt count, so parking never uses up retries. The park is uniform between `SLOW_PARK_MIN_MS` (2 s) and a window that widens by 20 ms for each queued slow job, capped at `JOBS_SLOW_PARK_MAX_MS` (60 s), so refused jobs do not come due together and a large send is not refetched and refused every second. Each park counts `jobs.slow.parked`. The other slots stay free for fast work. Fast work is not capped: it may use every slot, including the slow share when no slow work is running.

`claimSlotOrRequeue` also keeps a job at its priority when BullMQ does not. Stalled-job recovery and a manual retry (`job.retry()`, `queue.retryJobs()`, the Bull Board retry button) put a job on the plain wait list whatever its priority, ahead of all fast work. A job with a priority can legitimately start only when the plain wait list is empty, so a prioritized job that starts while fast work is waiting is moved back with `job.moveToWait`, which returns it to its priority band. Automatic retries and delayed promotion already keep the priority.

The slot share needs no shared state: every worker applies the same fraction to its own concurrency, so the fleet-wide share follows.

The slow slot is released in `processJob`'s `finally` however the handler ends, and a slow job's finish, success or failure, stamps the lane's idle clock (`recordSlowFinished`). A Redis error while stamping is logged and never fails the job.

<!-- unit doc:docs/jobs.md#fast-and-slow-lanes/pressure-one-budget-divided-by-lane -->
**Source:** `docs/jobs.md` § Fast and Slow Lanes › Pressure: One Budget, Divided by Lane (in "Jobs")

##### Pressure: One Budget, Divided by Lane

The overflow buffer's depth budget (`JOBS_MAX_QUEUE_DEPTH`) is shared by both lanes and counts everything waiting or running (`waiting + prioritized + active`) plus the slow jobs the lane deferred into `delayed`. Slow jobs — BullMQ's count for the slow priority band plus those deferred slow jobs — may fill only `JOBS_SLOW_QUEUE_DEPTH_FRACTION` of it. Each lane has its own overflow flag:

- **Fast** spills when the whole budget is full.
- **Slow** spills when its share is full, or when the whole budget is.

The drain refills fast rows up to the budget's free room, then slow rows up to what is left of both the budget and the slow share — batched, one read and one delete per lane per pass. Each lane's flag clears below its own low-water once none of its rows wait. Every slow row re-enters BullMQ at the slow priority.

###### The Deferral List

While the slot share has a send parked, nearly all of it sits in BullMQ's `delayed` set at any moment. A count that skipped `delayed` read a queued send as an empty lane: the drain admitted past the slow share and every signal read zero. But `delayed` cannot simply be counted — it also holds scheduled cron repeats, backoff retries and deliberately delayed fast jobs, and BullMQ keeps it as one set ordered by due time with no priority to count by.

So the slow lane keeps its own list of the slow jobs it put there (`jobs/slowLaneSignals.ts`): a Redis sorted set per queue, `job:<queue>:slow:deferred`, of job ids scored by due time. A job goes on it when `claimSlotOrRequeue` parks it (recorded before `moveToDelayed`, so a parked job is never outside the count) or when a slow job is added with a delay (`enqueueOrSpill`, or the drain re-adding a delayed slow row), and comes off when a worker picks it back up — when `claimSlotOrRequeue` gives it a slow slot or sends it back as a line-jumper. Keyed by job id, so parking the same job again moves its score instead of counting it twice. The list is a signal, not part of delivery: a Redis error while writing it is logged and never fails or blocks the job.

It cannot go by due time: BullMQ promotes delayed jobs only when a worker fetches, and parked jobs were measured sitting in `delayed` 2–21 s past due, so a count by due-time band undercounts. An entry stays counted until a worker picks the job up; only one nobody picks up within `SLOW_DEFERRED_GRACE_MS` (five minutes) of its due time — a delayed job deleted by hand, say — stops counting, and the drain pass prunes it. The depth probe caps the list at BullMQ's own `delayed` count, because a listed job that was promoted and is waiting to be fetched is in the slow band too.

###### Slow-Lane Signals

The worker registers three observable gauges beside `messaging.queue.messages`, read from one snapshot (`readSlowLaneState`):

- `jobs.slow.queued` — the slow band plus the deferred slow jobs: the number the slow share is enforced against.
- `jobs.slow.deferred` — the deferred part alone: jobs parked by the slot share and delayed slow adds.
- `jobs.slow.idle_ms` — how long slow work has been queued without a slow job finishing. It is 0 while nothing slow is queued (reading it then clears the stamp, so the next send's clock starts when its work is first seen, not at a finish from an earlier send). A draining send keeps it near one job's duration; a climbing value while `jobs.slow.queued` is above 0 is a slow lane that is not moving — hung handlers, or no workers — which the queue depth alone cannot tell apart from a large send draining normally.

The counter `jobs.slow.parked` counts refusals by the slot share. The drain pass reads the same snapshot at the end of every pass, so the flag-settling decisions use the same depths the gauges show and the idle clock advances every ~2 s.

<!-- unit doc:docs/jobs.md#fast-and-slow-lanes/lane-configuration -->
**Source:** `docs/jobs.md` § Fast and Slow Lanes › Lane Configuration (in "Jobs")

##### Lane Configuration

Defined in the env schema (`apps/api/src/config/env.ts`) with defaults in `apps/api/.env.local.example`:

| Env var | Default | Description |
|---------|---------|-------------|
| `JOBS_WORKER_CONCURRENCY` | `10` | BullMQ worker concurrency |
| `JOBS_SLOW_SLOT_FRACTION` | `0.5` | Share of each worker's slots slow jobs may run in (at least one) |
| `JOBS_SLOW_QUEUE_DEPTH_FRACTION` | `0.5` | Share of `JOBS_MAX_QUEUE_DEPTH` slow jobs may fill before spilling |
| `JOBS_SLOW_PARK_MAX_MS` | `60000` | Longest park for a slow job refused by a full slot share (min `1000`); parks start at 2 s and widen by 20 ms per queued slow job |
| `EMAIL_SLOW_LANE_MIN_RECIPIENTS` | `25` | `sendEmail` fan-outs wider than this are slow |

<!-- unit doc:docs/jobs.md#fast-and-slow-lanes/validating-against-real-infrastructure -->
**Source:** `docs/jobs.md` § Fast and Slow Lanes › Validating Against Real Infrastructure (in "Jobs")

##### Validating Against Real Infrastructure

`apps/api/scripts/slowLaneCheck.ts` runs the whole path against real Redis, a real BullMQ worker pair, and Postgres, and exits non-zero on any failure. It enqueues a slow send of multi-second jobs through `enqueueJob`, waits until slow work fills its slot share, then injects fast jobs and asserts that slow work ran in exactly its share of slots and never more, that fast jobs started within `SLOW_LANE_CHECK_FAST_WAIT_MS` (p95), and that every slow job ran once. It then spills a send larger than the slow share (`SLOW_LANE_CHECK_SEND_JOBS`, 200, of `SLOW_LANE_CHECK_SEND_JOB_MS`, 5 s) to `JobOutbox` and lets the real drain loop meter it in. Every 250 ms it compares the slow count the lane enforces (`queueDepths().slow`) with the slow jobs actually in Redis (`prioritized + delayed`), and it counts parks from the queue's `delayed` events. It fails if the send does not exceed the share, if the drain lets more than 110% of the slow share into Redis, if the signal reads under 0.8 or over 1.25 of the truth, if a queued slow job is parked more than 1.1× once per `SLOW_PARK_MIN_MS`, if the slow slots are busy less than 80% of the send (parked jobs coming back too late leave slots idle), or if a payload is lost or runs twice. A hung-handler case holds one slow slot for 3 s with five slow jobs queued and fails unless `jobs.slow.idle_ms` reads at least 80% of the hang, never more queued than jobs exist, and 0 once the lane empties. It also checks that 200 jobs at `SLOW_LANE_PRIORITY` keep distinct scores and FIFO order (reporting the collision at `PRIORITY_LIMIT` beside it), and that a manually retried slow job runs after waiting fast work with its priority intact. Its polling loops stop through a shared object (`loops.isRunning`), never a captured `let` — under Bun a loop was observed reading a captured `let` flag stale for 30 s — and every teardown await runs under a 30 s deadline. It obliterates the queue and empties `JobOutbox`, so it refuses to run without `ENVIRONMENT=local` and `SLOW_LANE_CHECK_CONFIRM=wipe`:

```bash
bun run with test api env ENVIRONMENT=local SLOW_LANE_CHECK_CONFIRM=wipe \
  REDIS_URL=redis://localhost:6379/9 REDIS_BULLMQ_URL=redis://localhost:6379/9 JOBS_MAX_QUEUE_DEPTH=200 \
  bun apps/api/scripts/slowLaneCheck.ts
```

`apps/api/scripts/jobFlowCheck.ts` does the same for staged jobs and the collision policy, because the test suite's Redis mock cannot run BullMQ's flow, deduplication or parent scripts. Against real Redis and a real worker it fails unless a staged job parks in `waiting-children` while its leaves run, runs its stage once and `finish` once after the last leaf; a child that fails every attempt is retried and then lets its parent finish; a staged singleton skips a second enqueue while it is parked and its key frees once it finishes; superseding a staged job aborts its running children within two seconds, the replaced parent never runs `finish` and the aborted children never write; and a cron tick enqueues the real run while a second tick during that run is skipped. It obliterates the jobs queue, so it refuses to run without `ENVIRONMENT=local` and `JOB_FLOW_CHECK_CONFIRM=wipe`:

```bash
bun run with local api env JOB_FLOW_CHECK_CONFIRM=wipe \
  REDIS_URL=redis://localhost:6379/12 REDIS_BULLMQ_URL=redis://localhost:6379/12 \
  bun apps/api/scripts/jobFlowCheck.ts
```

Point `REDIS_URL` at your own Redis (`REDIS_PORT` in the root `.env`). `SLOW_LANE_CHECK_JOBS`, `SLOW_LANE_CHECK_JOB_MS`, `SLOW_LANE_CHECK_WORKERS`, `SLOW_LANE_CHECK_FAST_WAIT_MS`, `SLOW_LANE_CHECK_SEND_JOBS`, and `SLOW_LANE_CHECK_SEND_JOB_MS` vary the run. Setting `JOBS_SLOW_SLOT_FRACTION=1` removes the reservation and the fast-wait assertion fails.

<!-- unit doc:docs/jobs.md#overflow-buffer -->
**Source:** `docs/jobs.md` § Overflow Buffer (in "Jobs")

#### Overflow Buffer

A durable buffer in front of BullMQ. When queue depth crosses a cap, an overflow flag flips and `adhoc` enqueues spill to the `JobOutbox` DB table instead of Redis; a per-worker drain loop meters them back in as room frees up. Source: `apps/api/src/jobs/outbox/`.

`JobOutbox` rows persist the full re-enqueue intent: `handlerName`, a unique `jobId` (idempotent re-enqueue), `dedupeKey` (superseding lane; null for plain fan-out), `lane` (each lane waits for room in its own share of the depth budget — mirrors `data.lane`), `data` (`JobData`), `options` (`JobOptions`), and a drain-local `attempts` counter (distinct from `options.attempts`). The `id` is a time-ordered uuidv7, so `orderBy: { id: 'asc' }` is FIFO drain order.

##### Spill Routing

`shouldSpill(type, bypass, overflowing)` is a pure predicate: spill only when `type === 'adhoc' && !bypass && overflowing`. A flow child (an enqueue carrying `parent`, added by a staged job's `enqueueChildJob`) never counts as overflowing and always goes direct: the drain's re-add would lose its parent link. Cron and cronTrigger jobs always go direct — only `adhoc` jobs are ever buffered. On a direct `adhoc` add, `recordAddAndTripIfFull()` counts it into a rough per-process depth estimate (last probe + adds since, re-probed every `DEPTH_PROBE_MS` = 2s); reaching a cap forces a fresh probe and the flag trips on what it reads, so a 20k or 100k wave turns spilling on part-way through. A fast add forces that probe only at the total cap, a slow add at either cap, so a full slow lane does not put a probe on every fast enqueue. The drain tick also trips the flag from the depths it reads (`tripFromDepths`). If Redis refuses an add as out of memory (`noeviction`), the job spills instead of failing; flow children and `bypass`/cron jobs still throw.

##### Accumulator

`spillToOutbox` routes every spill (fan-out and superseding) through an in-memory accumulator that batches DB writes:

- Flush triggers: a spill with no flush in flight is written at once; while a flush is queued or running, spills wait and go out as one batch when it settles (group commit). Size (`flushMaxRows`, default 1000) still splits a large burst. There is no linger timer.
- Within a batch, superseding lanes (`handlerName`+`dedupeKey`) collapse to the latest row (`dedupeLatestPerLane`); null-`dedupeKey` rows are all kept.
- One txn per flush: plain rows via `createManyAndReturn({ skipDuplicates })`, superseding lanes via `upsert` (last-writer-wins, no silent drop).
- Resolves on COMMIT, never on accumulation — a crash in the flush window must not drop a job.
- `flushOutbox()` is the shutdown drain: called after intake stops, it persists every buffered row with retry (`SHUTDOWN_FLUSH_RETRIES`) and surfaces failures loudly.

##### Drain Loop

`startOutboxDrainLoop()` / `stopOutboxDrainLoop()` run a per-worker, in-process `setInterval` every ~2s (not a queued cron). Each tick (`runDrainOutboxPass`) runs under a Redis lock (`createLock`, `service: 'outbox-drain'`) so only one worker drains at a time, and the NX acquire skips a tick whose predecessor is still running. The interval is short so a lane whose share empties quickly — many short slow jobs — is refilled before its slots sit idle; a pass with nothing buffered is a lock attempt and a job-count read.

A pass:
1. Reads the lane depths (`queueDepths`). Fetches up to the budget's free room of non-quarantined **fast** rows oldest-first (FIFO) and re-enqueues them, re-claiming the supersede lane first when `dedupeKey` is set. A stored job id BullMQ would reject is replaced with a fresh one rather than failing forever.
2. Does the same for **slow** rows, up to what is left of the budget and of the slow share, re-adding each at the slow priority.
3. Deletes drained rows per lane in one statement; increments `attempts` on rows that failed re-enqueue. After `MAX_DRAIN_ATTEMPTS` (5) failures a row is quarantined (skipped) so a poison row at the head can't starve newer rows.
4. Reads the slow-lane snapshot (`readSlowLaneState`: prunes the deferral list, fresh lane depths, idle clock). Under the outbox mutex: clears each lane's flag once that lane is below its own low-water with no admittable row and no pending spill of that lane; resets quarantined rows to `attempts: 0` only when the queue is below low-water and neither lane has an admittable row or a pending spill.

The whole pass runs inside `withOverflowRenew` so a long pass can't let either flag's TTL lapse mid-tick.

##### Overflow Flag

One Redis key per lane — `job:overflow` (the whole budget) and `job:overflow:slow` (the slow share) — value = epoch ms when overflow began:

- Set-once via `NX` so re-trips keep the original start time (used by the stuck-overflow alert).
- Carries a TTL the drain renews each tick (`renewOverflow` / `withOverflowRenew` heartbeat) — survives between ticks, self-clears if the drain dies.
- `warnIfOverflowStuck` logs when overflow has persisted past `overflowStuckMs` (drain not keeping up with arrivals).

##### Queue Depth Probe

`queueDepths()` returns `{ total, slow, slowDeferred }`: `slowDeferred` is the slow lane's deferral list capped at BullMQ's `delayed` count (see [The Deferral List](#the-deferral-list)); `total` counts `waiting + prioritized + active + slowDeferred`; `slow` counts the jobs waiting at `SLOW_LANE_PRIORITY` via BullMQ's `getCountsPerPriority` plus `slowDeferred`. The rest of `delayed` stays out — scheduled cron repeats and backoff retries are a standing floor, not pressure. Cached ~1s (`DEPTH_CACHE_MS`). Pass `fresh = true` to bypass the cache (used by the depth estimate's probe, `tripIfFull` and the drain). A job given an explicit priority between the lanes lands in `prioritized` and counts against the whole budget, not the slow share.

All `JobOutbox` writes — accumulator flushes AND the drain — run through one shared serialized queue (`flushQueue` / `runOnOutboxQueue`, via `createSerializedQueue`), so a flush and a drain can never touch the table concurrently.

##### Overflow Configuration

Defined in the env schema (`apps/api/src/config/env.ts`), read lazily through `outbox/config.ts`. In tests, `setEnvOverride` values for these knobs are parsed through the same schema fields (an invalid override keeps the parsed default):

| Env var | Default | Description |
|---------|---------|-------------|
| `JOBS_MAX_QUEUE_DEPTH` | `100000` | Depth cap that trips overflow |
| (derived) | `0.8 × cap` | Low-water mark for clearing |
| `JOBS_OUTBOX_FLUSH_MAX_ROWS` | `1000` | Accumulator size-flush threshold |
| `JOBS_OVERFLOW_TTL_MS` | `60000` | Flag TTL (drain heartbeats it) |
| `JOBS_OVERFLOW_STUCK_MS` | `300000` | Age before stuck-overflow warning |

<!-- unit doc:docs/jobs.md#cron-jobs -->
**Source:** `docs/jobs.md` § Cron Jobs (in "Jobs")

#### Cron Jobs

Stored in DB, scheduled as BullMQ job schedulers keyed by the row's `jobId` (`queue.upsertJobScheduler` / `removeJobScheduler`, never the deprecated `add({ repeat })` repeatable API). **A tick never runs its handler:** `processJob` hands a `cron` job to `enqueueCronRun`, which enqueues the real run through `enqueueJob` as a `cronTrigger` job carrying the row's `id`, with the tick's attempts and backoff (the row's `maxAttempts` / `backoffMs`, set on the scheduler template). The admin trigger (`triggerCronJob`) goes through the same `enqueueCronRun`. So a scheduled run and a manual trigger collide like any two enqueues (a singleton is deduplicated on the row; a superseding job takes over). A scheduler's job template cannot carry a deduplication id, which is why the tick hands off.

**Validation.** `validateCronJob` (`modules/admin/cronJob/validations/`) is the one answer to "can BullMQ schedule this row": the `jobId` passes `validateJobId` (a key with `:` is read as a legacy repeatable), the handler is registered, and BullMQ's own `defaultRepeatStrategy` computes a next run for the pattern. It throws a 422 `makeError`; it never returns a message. Only a row that ends up enabled is checked, so turning a row off always works. The row is checked once, at the entry point: the `cronJobSync` after-hook validates the written row (Prisma defaults included), and its throw rolls the write back; the boot reconcile validates the rows it reads. `upsertCronJobScheduler` trusts its row and does not re-check the handler.

**Sync.** Every scheduler write holds one Redis lock (`withCronJobsLock`, a `createLock` with a wait; admin writes answer 409 when it times out) and calls `lock.assertHeld()` (on `createLock`'s `Lock`) before each write, which throws `LockLostError` once `lock.isWithinLease()` is false; the API error boundary answers it 409. After a create, update or upsert commits, the hook's `db.onCommit` sync re-reads the row under the lock and makes its scheduler match it (enabled upserts, disabled removes, a changed `jobId` removes the old key). There is no did-anything-change check: the sync is idempotent and always runs. A delete removes the scheduler inside the transaction before it commits, so a failed removal rolls the delete back. A failed sync throws out of `db.onCommit`, so the request errors; re-sending the same request repairs it (admin create is an upsert on `jobId`, and an update re-syncs even when nothing changed).

**Worker start.** `registerCronJobs` reconciles under the same lock (longer wait). An enabled row that fails `validateCronJob` is turned off — the one caller that catches the validator — in a single `updateManyAndReturn` (`enabled: false`, which the `cronJobSync` hook does not fire on) with an error log: fix it and re-enable it. It then upserts every remaining row's scheduler and removes every scheduler whose key is not a live row's `jobId` — schedulers left by deleted, disabled or renamed rows, and the md5-keyed repeatables older code registered. A failed upsert or a lost lease throws out of the pass before the sweep, so the sweep never removes a working legacy schedule whose replacement was never written, and the throw fails `initializeWorker`. Rolling back past the scheduler change double-fires every cron (md5 and `jobId` keys do not dedupe) until a worker on the newer code boots and sweeps.

The scheduler tests (`apps/api/src/jobs/tests/cronJobSchedulers.test.ts`, `apps/api/src/modules/admin/cronJob/tests/cronJobSchedulers.test.ts`) need a real Redis at `REDIS_BULLMQ_URL` (BullMQ's Lua cannot run on the in-memory mock); `useRealJobsQueue()` (`apps/api/tests/utils/realJobsQueue.ts`) points the `queue` singleton's scheduler methods at a randomly named queue there for each test, obliterates and closes it after the test, and throws rather than skips when the URL is missing.

##### System Cron Jobs (seeded)

The system's own jobs are rows in `packages/db/prisma/seeds/cronJob.seed.ts` with stable ids. The seed runner writes each record inside `db.txn`, so with the api seed (`bun run db:seed`, hooks registered) every deploy's seed brings `name`, `jobId`, `handler` and `description` back in line with the code and the hook moves the scheduler: renaming a handler is a code change plus a seed. `pattern`, `enabled`, `payload`, `maxAttempts` and `backoffMs` are admin-tunable in superadmin, so the seed sets them on insert only (`updateOmitFields`).

##### Cron Patterns (UTC)

All cron patterns run in **UTC timezone**. Examples:

| Pattern | Schedule (UTC) |
|---------|----------------|
| `0 0 * * *` | Daily at midnight |
| `0 */6 * * *` | Every 6 hours |
| `0 9 * * 1-5` | Weekdays at 9am |
| `*/15 * * * *` | Every 15 minutes |

##### CronJob Model

| Field | Description |
|-------|-------------|
| `jobId` | BullMQ idempotency key (prevents duplicate registrations) |
| `name` | Human readable name (unique) |
| `description` | Optional description of what the job does |
| `pattern` | Cron expression (UTC) |
| `handler` | Handler name from registry |
| `payload` | JSON data for handler |
| `enabled` | Toggle on/off |
| `maxAttempts` | Retry attempts on failure |
| `backoffMs` | Exponential backoff base delay |
| `createdById` | Optional FK to User who created the job |

##### Admin Routes

```
# Ad-hoc Jobs
POST   /api/admin/job              # Enqueue ad-hoc job (options.lane overrides the lane)

# Cron Jobs
GET    /api/admin/cronJob          # List all
POST   /api/admin/cronJob          # Create
GET    /api/admin/cronJob/:id      # Read one
PATCH  /api/admin/cronJob/:id      # Update
DELETE /api/admin/cronJob/:id      # Delete
POST   /api/admin/cronJob/:id/trigger  # Run immediately (optional body { lane })
```

##### JobType Values

| Type | Description |
|------|-------------|
| `cron` | The BullMQ job scheduler tick; it only enqueues a `cronTrigger` run |
| `cronTrigger` | A cron row's real run, scheduled (from a tick) or manual (admin trigger) |
| `adhoc` | One-off job |

`type` gates overflow routing: only `adhoc` jobs ever spill to the buffer; `cron`/`cronTrigger` always go direct to BullMQ. See [Overflow Buffer](#overflow-buffer).

#### BullBoard

Web UI for monitoring and managing BullMQ jobs at `/bullBoard`.

##### Access

| Environment | Auth | URL |

| Local | None required | `<API_URL>/bullBoard` |
| Non-local | Basic auth required | Requires credentials |

```env
BULL_BOARD_USERNAME=admin
BULL_BOARD_PASSWORD=secret
```

##### Error Boundaries

**BullBoard:**
| Scenario | Behavior |
|----------|----------|
| Local, no credentials | Enabled without auth |
| Non-local, no credentials | Disabled (logs warning) |
| Non-local, with credentials | Enabled with basic auth |

**Job Worker:**
| Scenario | Behavior |
|----------|----------|
| Unknown handler name | Logs error, throws (job fails) |
| Handler throws | Logs error, re-throws (BullMQ retries based on `attempts`) |
| Handler parks (`WaitingChildrenError`, slot-gate `DelayedError`/`WaitingError`) | Span ends OK with outcome `waiting`; not logged as a failure; BullMQ moves the job |
| Test environment | Worker skipped entirely |
| Graceful shutdown | Waits for active jobs, closes connections |

##### Features

- View all queues and jobs
- Monitor job status (waiting, active, completed, failed)
- Inspect job data and errors
- Retry failed jobs
- Clean completed/failed jobs
- Pause/resume queues

<!-- unit doc:docs/signet-readme.md#preface -->
**Source:** `docs/signet-readme.md` § (preface) (in "@inixiative/signet")

### @inixiative/signet

> Part of [inixiative](https://www.inixiative.com), technology for cooperation. See [all the projects](https://github.com/inixiative).

Pass-through execution with tracking and audit. A Signet is how anything uses an integration through Kingdom: a revocable pass on the owner's terms. Kingdom decides who may grant and use one with [`@inixiative/permissions`](https://github.com/inixiative/permissions); a grant's lens is [json-rules](https://github.com/inixiative/json-rules). This package presents Kingdom Signets.

A **Signet** is Kingdom's only grant for using integrations. It has an owner and no integration of its own: it names resources, each on its own integration, with their operations, lens and limits, and it can be revoked. Its grantee is a user or an integration, for example a paired Foundry or a machine's local Archive. The grantee presents it with an access token plus a DPoP proof signed by its device key (RFC 9449).

This package is the one implementation of that protocol, shared by Kingdom (which verifies) and Archive, Foundry, Oracle and KCP (which present):

- `contracts`: the wire schemas: keys, grants (operation picks, lens layers), proposals, pairing requests, delivered credentials, `describe` and `execute`, and the conversation frames.
- `proof`: create and verify DPoP proofs (ES256, nonce-bound, access-token-bound).
- `files`: private 0600 JSON files for keys and credentials.
- `client`:
  - an **Installation** (a local Foundry, Archive or Oracle) is an actor known to Kingdom by its key: `registerInstallation`, then `requestRegistration` asks for what it needs (the owner it expects, by organization id or slug, and resources by id or by kind and name, with their operations) and returns a review code a person claims in Kingdom (a `registerIntegration` Inquiry), where the review opens with that owner and those resources selected, then `collectSignet` and `saveCollectedSignet`. `installationInquiries`, `installationSignets`, `cancelInstallationInquiry`, `enrollInstallationSignet` and `rotateInstallationKey` act as the installation. `requestSignetEntitlement` asks for more on a Signet the installation already holds (resources by id or by kind, projects by id, and a reason): Kingdom sends a `signetEntitlement` Inquiry to the person who issued the Signet, and approval adds what they approve, never more than asked, as a new revision of the same Signet; one request is open per Signet, and its `reviewUrl` is also on the installation's inquiries;
  - `pairInstallation` does the whole pairing (register, request, wait on the socket, confirm the owner, collect) and `holdInstallationSignets` keeps one credential file per Signet the installation's integrations hold, enrolling later grants and re-enrolling when Kingdom no longer reports the file's enrollment as current (a rotated key, a revoked or expired enrollment). It never deletes a file: a Signet missing from a snapshot (a paused integration) keeps its file;
  - `InstallationSocket`, Kingdom's live line to an installation: it proves the key, receives a snapshot of the installation's inquiries and Signets on connect and on every change, keeps the installation's integrations marked online, advertises its viewer URL, and polls the same reads while the socket is down;
  - a **person or their agent** acts as themselves with a Kingdom API token plus a proof from its key: `requestSignet` asks for a Signet over the resources it names (a `signetRequest` Inquiry, approved at once when the caller manages every integration it asks on), `awaitSignet` polls `collectSignet` until it is approved, and `enrollSignet` enrolls the key on a Signet an owner granted directly (`owner/grant`). `saveCollectedSignet` writes either result next to the key;
  - `installation`: the layout every installation shares, under one root per product (a Foundry's `kingdom/`, `~/.kcp`): one directory per Kingdom host with its key and one file per Signet (`installationPaths`, `installationDirectory`, `signetCredentialFile`, `heldCredentials`, and `heldSignetCredential` for one file: null when it is missing or an older client wrote it), `privateDirectory`, and `defaultInstallationName(product)`. `listedSignets`, `heldSignetFile` (enrolling again a Signet whose file is missing or unreadable, while Kingdom lists it) and `withdrawRegistration` read and act on it. `holdPersonSignets` enrolls the key on Signets issued to a person, under the same per-directory `withHoldLock` as `holdInstallationSignets`, so a person login and an installation sync never enroll over each other;
  - `SignetHolders`, a cache of each held Signet's `access/describe` (with its `holder`), keyed by credential file or by the caller's own `keyOf`, refreshed after `stale()`;
  - `SignetClient`, which renews its access token and signs each call: `describe`, `execute`, task settlement, and the run actions a Foundry uses for inference (`resolveRun`, `delegateRun`, `renewRun`, `revokeRun`), and for a subscription run `releaseSubscription`, `reportSubscriptionLimits` and `reportCredentialRejected` (the provider rejected the login a release handed out).

```ts
import { holdInstallationSignets, InstallationSocket, pairInstallation, SignetClient } from '@inixiative/signet';

const paired = await pairInstallation({
  url: kingdom, root: dataDir, kind: 'archive', name: 'Laptop Archive', sourceId,
  terms: {
    name: 'Laptop Archive', lifecycle: 'ongoing', expiresAt: null, maxRequests: null,
    owner: { ownerModel: 'Organization', organization: 'inixiative' },
    resources: [{ resourceKind: 'archiveLibrary', operations: { picks: ['sessions.write'] } }],
  },
  onReview: ({ review }) => console.log(`Approve in Kingdom: ${review}`),
  confirmOwner: async ({ ownerName }) => confirm(`Pair with ${ownerName}?`),
});

new InstallationSocket({
  url: kingdom,
  keyFile: paired.keyFile,
  onSnapshot: ({ signets }) => holdInstallationSignets(kingdom, paired.keyFile, paired.directory, signets),
}).start();

const signet = await SignetClient.fromFile(paired.credentialFile);
// paired.integrationId is the integration this installation became, from the approved registration
await signet.execute({ integrationId: paired.integrationId, operation: 'sessions.write', input: { resourceId, snapshot, previousDigest: null } });
```

A person's agent, with an API token minted in Kingdom:

```ts
import { awaitSignet, enrollSignet, generateSignetKey, requestSignet, saveCollectedSignet, SignetClient, writePrivateJson } from '@inixiative/signet';

await writePrivateJson(keyFile, generateSignetKey());
const { requestId, reviewCode } = await requestSignet(kingdom, keyFile, apiToken, {
  name: 'Research agent', lifecycle: 'ongoing', expiresAt: null, maxRequests: null,
  resources: [{ resourceModel: 'IntegrationResource', integrationResourceId, operations: { picks: ['documents.read'] } }],
});
const collected = await awaitSignet(kingdom, keyFile, requestId); // or, for a granted Signet:
// const collected = await enrollSignet(kingdom, keyFile, apiToken, { signetId, expectedRevision, name: 'Research agent' });
await saveCollectedSignet(credentialFile, kingdom, keyFile, collected);
const signet = await SignetClient.fromFile(credentialFile);
await signet.describe();
```

<!-- unit doc:docs/signet-readme.md#grants -->
**Source:** `docs/signet-readme.md` § Grants (in "@inixiative/signet")

#### Grants

A Signet revision grants rows (`grantResourceSchema`), each naming one resource or a scope, false polymorphic on `resourceModel`:

- **`IntegrationResource`**: `full`, or `operations` (the resolved leaves; absent when `full`), and `lens` (json-rules layers). `full` reaches everything the resource offers, now and as its catalog grows, capped live by the integration's baseline. It is a different axis from `Integration.full` / `Token.full`, which let a delegate act with its owner's whole authority.
- **`Integration`**: a scope, not one resource: the same `full` / `operations` / `lens` / `where` on every resource of `kind` on the integration, now and later, or with `projectId` only those in that Kingdom Project. Which scope a row names is what was granted (Aron, 2026-11-14: per-conversation is the usual grant, "but if you want to, you can do project-scoped, the whole Foundry, or the whole integration level"); nothing that reads a grant may assume a row names one resource. What a row reaches is Kingdom's to answer. Its `projectId` narrows which resources the row reaches; that is not the `Project` row below, which says where the Signet may be used. Its `where` is an entitlement condition, positive only, as on a resource row.
- **`Project`**: a Kingdom project the Signet may be used in. Nothing else: no `full`, operations or lens.

**Operation picks.** A provider's catalog is a flat list of dotted leaf keys per resource kind (`commits.read`, `events.pull_request.review_requested`). A party asks with `operationPickSchema`: `{ full: true }` or `{ picks }`, each pick a leaf or a prefix ending `.*` (`commits.*`, `events.pull_request.*`). `pickCovers(pick, leaf)` is the one rule for what a pick takes: a pick ending `.*` takes every leaf under its prefix, and any other pick takes the leaf of exactly that key, so a branch is always written with `.*`. `resolveOperationPicks(leaves, pick)` resolves picks to leaves once, when the grant is saved (a pick that reaches nothing throws `OperationPickError`, code `unknown_operation_pick`), so a later catalog addition reaches only `full` rows. `operationTree(leaves)` derives the nested tree a grant UI offers, every node with the pick that takes it. `narrowsOperations(inner, outer)`: a full `outer` contains everything, and a full `inner` under an `outer` that is not full is never a narrowing. `permitsOperation(scope, operation)` answers one operation; `scopeRefusal(scope, catalog, refusal)` runs a per-operation refusal over every catalog operation a row reaches (all of them when full, so re-run it when the catalog grows).

**Lens.** A grant row's lens is its own json-rules layers over the resource kind's operations lens, which Kingdom generates from its catalog under `provider:kind` (`operationsLens({ model, operations, rowModel, rowModels })`): the anchor is the kind's operations, each dotted segment of an operation a relation (the same shape as a Prisma map, nesting included), and each operation a list of the rows it reads (`ArchiveDocument`, `Thread`, `RepositoryCall`, `IntegrationEvent`). Relations are off until a layer turns them on, so a layer turns on the branches it keeps (`everyBranch(operations, leafNarrowing?)`) and narrows a row shape everywhere with `mapDefaults` (`rowModelLayer(operations, row, narrowing)`: a `where` filters rows; picks and omits trim the shape), or one branch through `root.relations` (`narrowingAtOperation(operation, narrowing)`); a row with no layers reads every branch. A party writes one layer (`lensLayerSchema`, a json-rules narrowing without its parent); Kingdom stores it as a `StoredLens` record (`storedLensLayerSchema`) under the base, an approver's layer under the request's, so every layer ANDs and an approver can only narrow. `composeGrantLens(baseId, base, storedLayers)` composes a row's layers over the base (json-rules `composeLens`, which validates each layer and the order of the chain) and throws `GrantLensError` when they don't parse, aren't one chain, or don't compose; `rowsThroughLens(lens, operation, rows)` reads an operation's rows through the result. Kingdom and a host both use these two. The base's id is `baseLensId(provider, kind)`.

A `where` that filters rows goes at the operation's own branch. One above it (on the root, or on a branch that holds several operations) is over the whole list, so it would show every row as soon as one matched; `composeGrantLens` refuses it. `conditionAtOperation(operation, condition)` writes a call's own filter as a rule for json-rules `validateRuleInLens` and is never a lens `where`. A lens `where` may use negated operators: it shapes what comes back and decides no permission.

Rows are read at an operation's branch: `operationRecord(operation, rows)` nests them for `projectRows` and `operationRows(record, operation)` reads them back. The refusals below read a `GrantLens`: the row's own layers plus `projectLens` of them composed over the base, at each operation's branch (`projectionVisit`, `projectionFilters`, `projectionShows`). A `GrantLens` describes one row. What a holder reaches in the end is Kingdom's to work out, and nothing here names another Signet, a budget or a path. The row an operation reads: `repositoryCallRow(input)` (`{ sha }`) for a repository call, `threadRow(threadId)` (`{ id }`) for a conversation's thread.

**Where.** A resource ask's `where` (`grantWhereSchema`) is the incoming side: a positive json-rules condition over the call (its input fields, such as `objectId`), which Kingdom checks before the call runs. This package refuses an empty or malformed one, an `all` or `any` that is empty or lists a bare `true` or `false` (at any depth), a non-positive one (json-rules `validateRule(where, { positive: true })`: no negated operator, since a `where` decides permission) and one longer than `grantWhereLimit` (16,000) characters as JSON. `equals null` is json-rules' "no value" form and is accepted: it admits a call that leaves the field out. A grant view (`signetGrantSchema`) carries the row's `where` whole, as the condition its calls must meet (`storedWhereSchema`). It is read as it is, whatever its size, so a holder never loses its own row over it; checking it is Kingdom's, at admission, and a holder never gates on it. The lens is the outgoing side. A grant that pins commits sends both: `objectId in […]` as its `where`, and the same ids as its lens pin.

**Owner.** A request may name the one owner it asks (`namedOwnerSchema`): the ids its model is keyed by (`ownerIdFields`) and every other id present and null, among `userId`, `organizationId`, `spaceId` and `integrationId`. A Signet's owner is one of the five owner models or an Integration in its own right (`signetOwnerModelSchema`), which is keyed by `integrationId` alone. The owner a holder reads back (`ownerRefSchema`, on a collected or held Signet) is still one of the five.

What a party asks for (`signetResourceSchema` by id, `requestedResourceSchema` by id or by kind on the integration it names with `integrationId`) carries picks and its own lens layer. By kind, `externalId` names one resource of that kind (a conversation's thread id); without it the ask reaches every resource of the kind on the integration. An Installation registering asks by id or by kind alone (`registeredResourceSchema`): the integration it becomes does not exist yet. What a holder reads (`signetGrantSchema`) is the stored row plus the resource's `kind`, the `integrationId` and, where the holder acts by it, its `externalId` of the integration it is on; a call names that integration (`execute({ integrationId, … })`).

<!-- unit doc:docs/signet-readme.md#declared-operations -->
**Source:** `docs/signet-readme.md` § Declared operations (in "@inixiative/signet")

#### Declared operations

An integration whose operations Kingdom executes generically declares them here, one module per resource kind: `threads.ts` for a Foundry's `conversation` resources, `archive.ts` for an Archive's `archiveLibrary`, `github.ts` for a GitHub `repository` (reads by object id). Each declares its operation enum, display names and the input each operation takes. `declaredOperationSchema` and `operationInputSchemas` join them (operation names are unique across contracts), `operationInputKeys(operation)` gives the `access/execute` keys an operation takes besides `resourceId` and `limit`, and `operationInputFromAccess(operation, input)` picks and parses exactly those. Kingdom's catalog, its input check and its dispatch read these, so a new operation is added here first.

- **Archive** (`archiveLibrary`): `documents.read`, `documents.search`, `sessions.write`, `sessions.delete`. `archiveSourceOperations` (`sessions.write`, `sessions.delete`) are a paired local Archive acting on its own sessions: Kingdom binds them to its `sourceId`, so their grant takes no lens. `archiveLensRefusal(operation, lens)` says why a grant can't carry its lens (search needs content over every document: no `where` at its branch, `content` shown there), and `archiveGrantRefusal(scope, lens)` checks a whole row.
- **GitHub** (`repository`): `commits.read`, `trees.read`, `blobs.read`. A grant pins commits with a `where` over the call's `objectId` (what may be asked) and a lens pin over the `RepositoryCall` rows' `sha` (what comes out); reading a commit never reaches its tree, so `repositoryLensRefusal(operation, lens)` (and `repositoryGrantRefusal(scope, lens)` for a row) refuses trees and blobs whose branch the lens filters.

<!-- unit doc:docs/signet-readme.md#agent-conversations -->
**Source:** `docs/signet-readme.md` § Agent conversations (in "@inixiative/signet")

#### Agent conversations

A conversation wraps a host Foundry's main thread (Kingdom `docs/AGENT-CONVERSATIONS.md`, Foundry `docs/reference/CONVERSATIONS.md`). It is an integration resource of the host Foundry (Aron, 2026-11-14): one `conversation` resource per shared thread (`conversationResourceKind`), its `externalId` the thread's id. A member is a Signet with an entitlement on that resource; Kingdom admits each call and relays it over the host's Installation socket, and stores no post.

- **Calls and permissions.** The resource's catalog has two parts. The calls (`threadOperationSchema`): `thread.read`, `thread.prompt`, `thread.floor`, `prompt.resolve`. And the permissions (`conversationPermissionSchema`), which a grant picks like any operation and nothing calls, as with the `events.*` leaves: `member.log` (read the whole conversation, not only its own posts and the sends to it), `member.wake` (a post wakes the host's agent instead of riding its next turn), `member.take` (take the floor without being given it), `member.agent` (bring its own agent, not only itself as a person; Kingdom cannot tell a person's post from an agent's, so the host counts on it and nothing enforces it), `agent.instruct` (its posts are instructions, not data), `agent.read` and `agent.act` (what the host's agent may do on its word without asking the host). None is a declared operation, so none can be called, and they sit on their own branches (`member.`, `agent.`), so `thread.*` picks the calls alone. `conversationActLevel(permissions)` reads the act level from the highest held: `full` with `agent.act`, `read` with `agent.read`, else `ask`. Approving a request narrows like any operation selection. Kingdom sends the host the permissions the Signet holds on the conversation on every frame (`permissions`, each admitted on its own, as an event leaf is), beside the conversation's `threadId`; no call's input names the thread, because the call's resource is the conversation. What is the host's own choice about a member (whether its sends to them wait for review, `conversationOutboundSchema`; whether an agent speaks or listens) is the host's setting and is not on the grant. A holder reads a conversation resource's `externalId` on its grant rows and in `describe` (Kingdom sends no other kind's provider id): it is the thread id its stream opens by (`socket.open(threadId)`), while its calls name the resource (`resourceId`).
- **Join requests** may name a conversation by kind: `requestSignet` takes `{ resourceKind: 'conversation', integrationId, externalId, operations }`, the Foundry's integration and the thread's id, and Kingdom resolves it before review. A `conversation` ask without a thread id is refused: it would reach every conversation of that Foundry.
- **Per-entry reads.** `installationInquiries`, `installationSignets`, the socket snapshot and `describe` read each entry on its own. An entry this package can't read is dropped and listed in `dropped`, and the rest is kept. Inside a Signet, resources are read one by one: a resource this package can't read is dropped, and the Signet stays, so an installation never loses a held Signet, or mistakes a member for revoked, over one resource. The snapshot carries `hostedSignets` (members of this Foundry's conversations) and `hostedSignetRequests` (join requests aimed at its integrations, each requester marked `inOrg` or `outside` by Kingdom, so the host can start the review from its default for that audience); a hosted Signet's `recipient` carries its `audience` too (`owner`, `inOrg` or `outside`): the host's settings for that member start from it, and `owner` (the recipient is the person who owns the integration; never an Integration recipient, never on an integration an organization or space owns) is the only thing that makes a Signet the owner's own client, since anyone may be granted `prompt.resolve`; a hosted request's `resourceHandles` give the thread id of each conversation it names; held Signets carry their `resources`.
- **Host.** `InstallationSocket` takes `threads`, one handler per operation (`thread.read`, `thread.prompt`, `thread.floor`, `prompt.resolve`, `thread.subscribe`), answering `threadResult(...)` or `threadRefused(code)`. A frame this package can't read is refused `invalid_request` before any handler runs. `thread.subscribe` answers with the member's view and the `journalSeq` it was taken at, and the subscription starts there: `appendThread(subscriptionId, entry)` holds entries pushed meanwhile and never sends one twice. Each append carries a dense per-subscription `seq` (a filtered view skips journal entries, so `journalSeq` can't reveal loss); an entry that can't be sent still spends its `seq`, so Kingdom sees the gap and the member resyncs. A subscription ends on `thread.unsubscribe`, when Kingdom stops re-asserting its lease (`thread.lease`; dropped 90 s after the last one, so one late 45 s sweep is survived), or when the socket drops.
- **Member.** An outside agent holds its live views with `SignetSocket`: it authenticates as its Signet's presentation (`authenticateSignet`, a proof bound to `POST /api/v1/access/signetSocket` with `ath`), renews it before the five-minute token expires (`renewPresentation`), and opens one `accessThread` stream per thread: a snapshot, then appends, with Kingdom's `seq`/`resync` rules. Frames are handled in order, one open is in flight per stream, and Kingdom's close carries the reason: after a revision the stream reopens under the new revision, while the host is offline it retries with backoff, when the presentation lapsed the socket re-presents and reopens, and on revocation or expiry it ends (`onClosed`). Posts are separate `execute` calls (`thread.prompt`), each admitted and metered. A Foundry holding a conversation Signet opens the same streams over its Installation socket (`threadStreams`, `openThread`).

```ts
import { SignetClient, SignetSocket } from '@inixiative/signet';

const signet = await SignetClient.fromFile(credentialFile);
const socket = new SignetSocket({
  client: signet,
  onSnapshot: ({ threadId }, view) => show(threadId, view.entries),
  onEntry: ({ threadId }, entry) => append(threadId, entry),
  onClosed: ({ threadId }, reason) => console.log(`left ${threadId}: ${reason}`),
});
socket.open(threadId);
socket.start();
await signet.execute({
  integrationId,
  operation: 'thread.prompt',
  input: { resourceId, postId: Bun.randomUUIDv7(), text: 'The role you wanted opened' },
});
```

#### Integration events

An integration that receives its provider's events (GitHub, Slack, Linear) streams each one to the Signets whose grant picks its kind (Kingdom `docs/INTEGRATION-EVENTS.md`). Event kinds are operation leaves (`events.<event>.<action>`, `eventOperationKey`), picked like any other, and they are streamed, never executed.

- **Channels.** A channel is one resource a Signet holds event operations on. `describe` and each held Signet of the Installation snapshot carry `eventChannels` (`eventChannelMapSchema`): per integration `{ id, provider, name }`, per channel `{ resourceId, kind, name, events, stream }`. They are read per entry: an integration or channel this package can't read is dropped and listed in `dropped`, and the Signet is kept. The field is absent when Kingdom sent none (a Kingdom before integration events), which says nothing about what the Signet holds.
- **Holding a channel.** `SignetSocket` takes `eventStreams` (`EventStreamHandlers`) and holds a channel by its resource: `openEventChannel(resourceId)`, `leaveEventChannel(resourceId)`, `heldEventChannels()`. `InstallationSocket` takes the same for the Signets an installation holds, keyed `{ signetId, resourceId }`. Each channel is one `accessEvents` stream on the socket that carries thread streams, run by the same code (`DataStreams`), wired once for both sockets (`HolderStreams`), so Kingdom's close means the same: after a revision of the holder's Signet the channel reopens under the new revision (at once; with backoff when Kingdom refuses that reopen as `revised` too), when the presentation lapsed the socket authenticates again on a new connection and reopens, a dropped socket reopens what it held, Kingdom's `resync` (its own subscriber reconnected) reopens it, a close it is reopened after is reported first (`onReopening(channel, reason)`), a lost connection is reported once (`onDisconnected` on the socket), an offline host is retried with backoff, and on revocation, expiry or a refused open the channel ends (`onClosed`). `reopenedCloseReasons` lists the closes a stream is reopened after (`revised`, `presentationExpired`, `hostOffline`; `closeIsReopened(reason)`), and `onReopening` reports only those. A close reason is about the holder's own Signet: `revoked`, `revised`, `expired` and `enrollmentRevoked` never describe anything else, and a change elsewhere closes a stream as `unauthorized`, with no further reason, only once nothing admits it. A refused presentation is reported as a `SignetPresentationRefused` error. Opens are paced, ten per two and a half seconds for each kind of stream (`openBurst`, `openWindowMs` on either socket), because Kingdom closes a socket that sends more than 120 frames in ten seconds: a holder of many channels sees them open over a few windows, after every reconnect too. Thread streams are paced the same way. Leaves are not paced, so leaving more than about a hundred streams in one go costs a reconnect.
- **Live only.** A channel's snapshot is always empty and nothing is replayed. `onEvent(channel, { type, event }, seq)` receives each event as that channel's Signet projects it, from the moment Kingdom opens the channel (`onOpened`, again after every reopen). A holder that is offline misses what is published meanwhile, as it does between a close and the reopen, and there is nowhere to read it back from.
- **Gaps.** A thread stream whose `seq` jumps reopens for a fresh snapshot, which holds what it missed. A channel's snapshot holds nothing, so every append that arrives is delivered, whatever its `seq`, and a `seq` that isn't the next one (a jump, or a count that went back) is reported: `onGap(channel, { after, seq })`, just before the event that showed it. A gap means one of two things this package can't tell apart: Kingdom's counter for the stream expired after 24 quiet hours and started again from the clock (nothing was lost), or appends in between never arrived (they are gone). A reconnect reports no gap; it shows as `onOpened`. Frames are handled one at a time, so a handler slower than Kingdom holds back the ones behind it: past `maxQueuedFrames` waiting (1,000 unless set on the socket) appends are dropped, reported once through `onError`, and show as a gap on a channel or a resync on a thread, at the next append or once the handlers have caught up.
- **Duplicates.** Nothing is deduped here: an event is delivered once per channel it arrives on. A holder with two Signets on one resource gets the event on both channels, each cut by its own Signet's lens, so the two bodies can differ. Every event carries `id`, a UUID Kingdom mints once per event, after it has dropped the provider's retried deliveries (which it does for three days, by the provider's delivery id). The `id` is the same on every channel the event reaches and a lens can't drop it, so a consumer that must act once dedupes on `event.id`.
- **What a lens can name.** An event reaches a holder as the `IntegrationEvent` row its Signet's lens projects. A layer at an `events.*` branch names only the row fields, `integrationEventFieldSchema`: `id`, `integrationId`, `provider`, `at`, `actor`, `scope`, `mentions`, `assignees`, `requestedReviewers`, `subject`, `excerpt` and `payload`, the provider's whole event as it arrived (a layer keeps or drops it whole). `id` is the row's identifier: a layer can filter on it and can never leave it out (Kingdom refuses a lens that does). `type` rides outside the projected body on every append, and the provider's delivery id (`eventId`) stays in Kingdom, so a layer that picks or filters on either does not compose.
- **Truncation.** Kingdom caps an append's size. When the projected event is over the cap, it arrives without `payload` and the append carries `truncated: true`; the other fields are whole. A holder that needs the full body reads it from the provider.

```ts
import { SignetClient, SignetSocket } from '@inixiative/signet';

const signet = await SignetClient.fromFile(credentialFile);
const { eventChannels = [] } = await signet.describe();
const socket = new SignetSocket({
  client: signet,
  eventStreams: {
    onEvent: ({ resourceId }, { type, event }) => notify(resourceId, event.id, type, event),
    onGap: ({ resourceId }, { after, seq }) => console.warn(`${resourceId}: seq ${after} -> ${seq}`),
    onClosed: ({ resourceId }, reason) => console.log(`stopped listening on ${resourceId}: ${reason}`),
  },
});
for (const { channels } of eventChannels)
  for (const channel of channels) socket.openEventChannel(channel.resourceId);
socket.start();
```
